name: EU AI Act — Risk Tiers & Obligations

applicability.trigger: Applies to providers placing an AI system on the market or putting it into service in the EU, and to deployers of AI systems located in the EU — with extraterritorial reach to a provider or deployer outside the EU whose AI system's output is used within the EU (Art. 2). The obligations that attach depend entirely on which risk tier the system falls into: a prohibited practice under Art. 5 may not be placed on the market at all; a high-risk system under Art. 6 and Annex III triggers the full Chapter III obligation set; a system covered by Art. 50 triggers transparency-only obligations; everything else is minimal-risk with no tier-specific obligations under this Act.
jurisdiction: Providers or deployers outside the EU/EEA whose AI system's output is used within the EU/EEA (extraterritorial scope, Art. 2)

required_elements.requirement: An AI system may not be placed on the market, put into service, or used if it falls into a prohibited category: subliminal or purposefully manipulative/deceptive techniques that materially distort behavior and cause significant harm; exploiting a person's age, disability, or socioeconomic vulnerability to materially distort their behavior harmfully; social scoring leading to unjustified detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts; assessing the risk of a person committing a criminal offense based solely on profiling or personality-trait assessment; untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV to build or expand a facial recognition database; inferring emotions in the workplace or in education (except for medical or safety purposes); biometric categorization to deduce race, political opinion, trade union membership, religious belief, or sexual orientation; and real-time remote biometric identification by law enforcement in publicly accessible spaces, except under narrow, judicially authorized exceptions.

An AI system is high-risk if it falls into one of eight Annex III categories: biometric identification/categorization/emotion recognition; management of critical infrastructure (digital infrastructure, road traffic, utilities); education and vocational training (admission, evaluation, monitoring); employment (recruitment, candidate evaluation, performance monitoring); access to essential services (public benefits eligibility, creditworthiness, insurance risk, emergency-call triage); law enforcement (risk assessment, polygraphs, evidence reliability, profiling); migration, asylum, and border control; and the administration of justice and democratic processes (judicial decision support, election-outcome influence).

A provider of a high-risk AI system must establish, implement, document, and maintain a risk management system as a continuous iterative process throughout the system's lifecycle, identifying and analyzing foreseeable risks, evaluating risks arising from post-market monitoring data, and adopting suitable risk-mitigation measures.

Training, validation, and testing data sets for a high-risk AI system must be subject to data governance practices appropriate to their intended purpose, including examination for possible biases and measures to detect, prevent, and mitigate them, and must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and, to the best extent possible, free of errors.

A provider must draw up technical documentation before a high-risk AI system is placed on the market, demonstrating compliance with Chapter III's requirements and providing authorities with the information needed to assess that compliance.

A high-risk AI system must technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over its lifetime, at a level enabling the system's operation to be traced back and supporting post-market monitoring.

A high-risk AI system must be designed to ensure its operation is sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, accompanied by instructions for use including its intended purpose, level of accuracy, and known limitations.

A high-risk AI system must be designed to enable effective oversight by natural persons during the period it is in use, through measures identified by the provider or implemented by the deployer, appropriate to the risks, level of autonomy, and context of use.

A high-risk AI system must be designed to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and to perform consistently in those respects throughout its lifecycle, including resilience against attempts to alter its use, outputs, or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities.

Providers and deployers of certain AI systems must disclose AI involvement to the people affected: a person must be informed they are interacting with an AI system unless this is obvious; AI-generated synthetic audio, image, video, or text must be marked as artificially generated or manipulated; a person exposed to an emotion-recognition or biometric-categorization system must be informed; and deepfake content, or AI-generated text published on matters of public interest, must be disclosed as such, subject to narrow exceptions.

A provider of a high-risk AI system must report a serious incident to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where it occurred. The general deadline is 15 days after the provider (or, where applicable, the deployer) establishes a causal link between the AI system and the incident, or the reasonable likelihood of such a link. That deadline shortens to immediately, and no later than 2 days, for a widespread infringement or a serious incident causing a serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure (Art. 3(49)(b)); and to no later than 10 days for a serious incident involving the death of a person.
Following a serious incident, the provider must perform the necessary investigations, including a risk assessment of the incident and corrective action, and cooperate with the competent authorities.

terms_of_art.meaning: A machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy, that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs — such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions — that can influence physical or virtual environments (Art. 3(1)).

A natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that develops an AI system (or has one developed) and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark.
A natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body using an AI system under its authority, other than for purely personal, non-professional use.

An AI system falling within an Annex III use-case category (or serving as a safety component of a product already subject to third-party conformity assessment), unless it falls within a narrow carve-out (e.g. performing a purely preparatory task or not materially influencing the outcome of a decision).

One of the eight practices enumerated in Art. 5 that may not be placed on the market, put into service, or used at all, regardless of risk-mitigation measures — distinct from a high-risk system, which may be used if its Chapter III obligations are met.

An incident or malfunctioning of an AI system that directly or indirectly leads to: (a) the death of a person, or serious harm to a person's health; (b) a serious and irreversible disruption of the management or operation of critical infrastructure; (c) the infringement of obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights; or (d) serious harm to property or the environment (Art. 3(49)).

name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) 1.0

applicability.trigger: Voluntary — an institution opts into assessment against this framework to structure AI risk management using a common vocabulary, often alongside EU AI Act compliance work or a procurement requirement that references it. Not a checklist of binding requirements; each function's outcomes are adopted, adapted, or explicitly deprioritized with a stated reason, the same way the NIST Privacy Framework's profiles work.

required_elements.requirement: A culture of AI risk management is cultivated and present: policies, processes, and accountability structures for managing AI risk are established across the system's lifecycle, including risk tolerance, workforce training, and third-party and supply-chain risk from externally sourced data, models, or components.

The context for a specific AI system is established: its intended purpose, benefits, and the risks it poses to individuals, groups, organizations, and society are identified and categorized before those risks are measured or managed.

Identified risks are analyzed, benchmarked, and monitored using quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods — including testing, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) for accuracy, bias and fairness, robustness, and explainability.

Resources are allocated to risks that have been mapped and measured, on a regular basis and informed by the GOVERN function, and the organization has a defined way to respond to, recover from, and communicate about an AI incident once one occurs.

terms_of_art.meaning: The composite of the probability of an event occurring and the magnitude of its consequences — a framing that, unlike a pure-harm definition, allows for both negative and positive impacts to be weighed.
Test, evaluation, verification, and validation — the set of activities under the MEASURE function that establish whether an AI system performs as intended, safely, and without unacceptable bias.

In this framework, an AI system that is valid and reliable, safe, secure and resilient, accountable and transparent, explainable and interpretable, privacy-enhanced, and fair with harmful bias managed — the characteristics the four functions are organized to support.
Anyone playing an active role in the AI system lifecycle, including the organizations and individuals that design, develop, deploy, operate, or evaluate an AI system.

applicability.trigger: Voluntary — an institution opts into assessment against this standard, typically to structure an AI management system (AIMS) for organizations that develop, provide, or use AI systems, or to demonstrate AI governance maturity to partners, regulators, or auditors. Follows the same high-level structure (clauses 4-10) shared across other ISO management-system standards (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001), extended with an AI-specific Annex A control set.

required_elements.requirement: The organization must establish, document, and communicate an AI policy setting out its objectives and principles for developing, providing, or using AI systems responsibly.
The organization must assess the impacts an AI system may have on individuals or groups — including foreseeable harms — before and during its use, as part of the management system's own risk process.
The organization must define and follow a lifecycle process for AI systems it develops or provides, covering design, development, verification, validation, deployment, operation, and retirement.

The organization must manage data used to develop, train, and evaluate an AI system — including its provenance, quality, and known limitations — as its own governed category of documented information.

The organization must provide interested parties (users, affected individuals, regulators) with information about an AI system sufficient to understand its intended purpose, capabilities, and limitations — the clause this project's `draft-model-card` skill most directly documents against.

The organization must maintain documented information required by this standard and by its own determination as necessary for the AI management system's effectiveness, controlled for availability, protection, and version currency.

terms_of_art.meaning: Artificial Intelligence Management System — the set of policies, processes, and controls an organization implements to govern how it develops, provides, or uses AI systems, structured the same way an ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS structures information security management.
A person or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by an AI system's development, provision, or use — broader than only the AI system's direct users.
